title: cosd
summary: Compute cosine of degree-valued inputs in MATLAB and RunMat.

gpu_support.notes: GPU inputs gather to the exact host reference path and the floating result is restored to the owning provider.

fusion.notes: Fusion is intentionally disabled for v1 because the WGSL `cos(x*pi/180)` form would lose MATLAB's exact-value guarantees at canonical angles.

description: `y = cosd(x)` evaluates cosine element-wise in degrees. MATLAB documents single and double real or complex arrays; RunMat mode additionally admits typed integers, logicals, and characters through explicit compatibility gates.
behaviors: Operates element-wise on scalars, vectors, matrices, and N-D tensors.
Single real and complex inputs preserve single output; double inputs preserve double output.

Typed integers are a RunMat-only extension. All eight real integer classes require exact binary64 representability before degree reduction and produce double output; aligned values above `flintmax` are accepted when their significant bits fit binary64.
Logical and character inputs are separately gated RunMat-only extensions and produce double output.
Returns exactly 0 at multiples of 90 and exactly ±1 at multiples of 180.
Returns exactly ±0.5 at multiples of 60 and 120.
Complex inputs delegate to the analytic extension of `cos` after scaling by `pi/180`; exact-value treatment for complex operands is deferred.
Output shape matches the input shape; non-finite inputs propagate as `NaN`.
String inputs are unsupported and raise a builtin-scoped error.
Table, timetable, tall, and distributed container inputs remain general RunMat container/runtime gaps rather than integer-storage gaps.

examples.description: Cosine of a canonical degree angle
Cosine of multiples of 90 returns exactly zero
Cosine of a vector of common angles

faqs.question: Why does `cosd(90)` return exactly zero?
faqs.answer: MATLAB guarantees an exact zero at multiples of 90 to avoid floating-point noise from `pi`. RunMat reduces the angle modulo 360 and short-circuits the canonical cases before delegating to `cos`.

faqs.question: Is `cosd(x)` equivalent to `cos(x*pi/180)`?
faqs.answer: Mathematically yes, but the floating-point result differs at canonical angles because `pi/180` is not exact in binary floating point. `cosd` returns the exact MATLAB values at multiples of 60, 90, 120, and 180.

faqs.question: Does `cosd` support arrays?
faqs.answer: Yes. Scalars, vectors, matrices, and N-D tensors are all handled element-wise; the shape of the input is preserved.
